The cactus sea squirt Boltenia echinata reaches an ultimate body length of approximately 4.6 centimeters [Li = approximately 4.6 centimeters], a size predicated on the assumption of a spherical body plan that yields an ultimate wet weight of about 51 grams [Wwi = about 51 grams]. This asymptotic mass, derived from volumetric calculations based on the maximum recorded diameter, provides a useful benchmark for comparing growth trajectories among solitary ascidians. Field surveys conducted in the cold waters of the North Atlantic have reported individuals approaching these dimensions, though local environmental conditions can lead to considerable variation. Comparatively, earlier work by Millar in 1970 suggested a more conservative maximum length of 2 centimeters for this species, a discrepancy that may reflect differences in population density, food availability, or sampling methodology across distinct geographic regions. The larger value documented more recently likely represents the true growth potential under favorable, resource-rich conditions, underscoring the plasticity inherent in the life history of Boltenia echinata.

Sexual maturation in Boltenia echinata is attained at a body length of approximately 0.7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 0.7 centimeters], a relatively modest size compared to the ultimate length of the species. This size at puberty indicates that reproductive activity commences well before somatic growth is complete, a strategy common among many solitary ascidians that allows individuals to contribute to the next generation even under variable or suboptimal conditions. The onset of gonadal activity at this length is a critical life history transition, marking the point at which energy is partitioned between further body growth and the production of gametes. Field observations suggest that individuals reaching this size typically have a functional reproductive system, although the exact timing may be influenced by local temperature regimes and food supply. The relatively small size at puberty, representing less than one-sixth of the maximum body length, implies a high reproductive potential early in life, which may be advantageous in dynamic or unpredictable benthic environments.

At a stable experimental temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the embryonic development of Boltenia echinata proceeds such that hatching occurs approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days] after fertilization. This period of incubation is consistent with the slow developmental rates characteristic of cold-water ascidians, where low temperatures decouple metabolic processes and prolong embryogenesis. The newly emerged larvae are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during their brief planktonic phase. Upon settlement and metamorphosis, the resulting juvenile has a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the estimated diameter of the newly metamorphosed individual. This small initial mass places the species among the smaller-bodied solitary ascidians at the onset of benthic life, necessitating a period of rapid feeding and growth to reach a size refuge from predation and physical disturbance.

Under the same thermal regime of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the maximum lifespan of Boltenia echinata in the wild has been estimated at approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years], a longevity that is notable among solitary ascidians of comparable body size. This duration is likely constrained by the energetic costs of reproduction and the gradual accumulation of senescent changes in the sessile adult. Field studies tracking tagged individuals have confirmed that few animals survive beyond this age, with natural mortality increasing sharply after the third year. The 4-year lifespan represents a relatively fast pace of life for an ascidian of its ultimate dimensions, perhaps reflecting a trade-off between early, high reproductive output and a shorter overall adult tenure. The oldest documented individuals in laboratory colonies have matched this field estimate, suggesting that the intrinsic physiological limit is not easily extended by benign captive conditions and that genetic programming plays a major role in determining longevity.

Field records of reproductive output in Boltenia echinata, maintained at 9 °C [T = 9 °C], indicate that a fully mature female can release approximately 9 to 10 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 9 to 10 eggs per day] when conditions are optimal, a rate that reflects the high energetic investment in gametogenesis. This daily fecundity is notable among its congeners and underscores the species' capacity for rapid population increase under favorable conditions. The maximum reproductive rate, translating to roughly 3500 eggs per year, is based on a provisional estimate derived from energetic considerations and is best considered an approximation. Spawning events are typically pulsed throughout the year, often synchronized with phytoplankton blooms or other environmental cues, which may modulate the actual daily output. Nevertheless, the overall high fecundity of Boltenia echinata, combined with its relatively early sexual maturation at 0.7 centimeters body length, contributes to a life history strategy that can quickly exploit transiently favorable benthic conditions.
